title: Software Integrity, Anti-Tamper and Fair Play
summary: This course taught how programs look from the inside, which is also how cheats and tampering work. This lesson takes the defender's side: why a game can never fully trust the client, why **server authority** is the foundation of fair online play, how to verify the integrity of your own files and updates with hashes and code signing, what client-side anti-tamper can and cannot do, and the legal, ethical and privacy limits that apply to both sides.
markdown:
## The client is in the player's hands Every technique in chapters 5 to 16 works on a program running on your own machine: reading its memory, changing its code, injecting a DLL, inspecting its traffic. A player can do all of that to a game on **their** machine. That leads to the most important rule of game security: > [!important] Never trust the client > Anything that runs on the player's computer can be read and changed by the player. Decisions that affect other players must be made, or at least checked, somewhere the player does not control. Client-side protection can make tampering slower and more obvious; it cannot make it impossible. Fair play in online games rests on design first and detection second. ## Server authority In an **authoritative server** design, clients send **inputs** ("move forward", "fire at this direction") and the server runs the simulation and decides the results. A modified client can still send inputs, but it cannot directly set its health, teleport, or award itself a score. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant C as Client participant S as Server (authoritative) C->>S: input: move right, tick 1042 S->>S: validate: speed, collisions, cooldowns S->>S: simulate the tick S-->>C: state: position, health, events Note over C: the client predicts locally for smoothness,
then corrects to the server's state ``` What the server validates: | Check | Example | |---|---| | **Physics limits** | A move longer than maximum speed times elapsed time is clamped or rejected (the practice task) | | **Rates and cooldowns** | No more shots than the weapon's fire rate allows | | **Visibility** | The server sends a player only what that player could legitimately see, so there is nothing hidden in memory to reveal | | **Game rules** | Items can only be used if owned; doors only opened if unlocked | | **Plausibility over time** | Statistics that are consistently beyond human limits are flagged for review, never banned automatically | For single-score games like Delve's leaderboard, the equivalent is submitting a **replay** (the seed and the inputs) instead of a score; the server re-simulates it deterministically and computes the score itself (the leaderboard threat in lesson 17.05). ## Integrity of your own files Separately from cheating, you need to know the code and data you ship are the code and data that run, and that updates come from you: - **Hash manifests**: a list of every shipped file with its SHA-256 hash. The launcher or updater checks files against it, which catches corruption and incomplete updates (lesson 3.08's checksums, made cryptographic). - **Code signing**: an Authenticode signature on your executables and DLLs (and the manifest) proves who published them and that they were not changed. Windows shows the publisher and SmartScreen builds reputation from it; drivers must be signed to load at all (lesson 16.01). - **Signed updates**: an updater verifies the signature of a downloaded update before installing it, so a compromised download server cannot push malicious code. - **Safe loading**: load DLLs only from your own folder with full paths (lesson 13.04), so a planted DLL is not picked up instead. ## What client-side anti-tamper does Commercial games add protection on the client. Understanding its purpose, at a high level, helps you design around it and judge its trade-offs: | Measure | Purpose | Limit | |---|---|---| | **Integrity checks** of the game's own code and data | Detect modified files or patched code | Runs on the same machine it is protecting | | **Obfuscation** | Make analysis (chapter 9) slower | Slows, never prevents | | **Detecting debuggers and injected modules** | Notice the tools of chapters 8 and 13 | False positives on legitimate software | | **Kernel-mode components** | Observe from a more privileged level | Very high trust demanded from players; a driver bug crashes their machine (chapter 16) | The cost side matters: kernel-level anti-cheat asks players to trust your code with full control of their computer, and some players reasonably refuse. Collect only what is needed, document what is collected, and remove the component when the game is uninstalled. ## The rules for both sides - **Terms of service and the law** apply. Modifying or analysing a game you do not own can break its licence, and creating or selling cheats for online games has led to lawsuits. Cheating in online games harms other players, and this course does not teach it. - **Fair-play enforcement must be fair**: decisions reviewed by humans, an appeal process, and evidence kept (the repudiation row in 17.05). - **Privacy**: anti-cheat that scans the player's machine is handling personal data and falls under laws such as the GDPR. - **Single-player modding** is a different matter: it harms no one, and many developers support it with official tools (chapter 13). ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Trusting client-reported results > "The client says it hit for 9999 damage" must never be believed. > [!warning] Sending hidden information to clients > If the client receives every enemy position, a modified client can show them. Send only what can be seen. > [!warning] Relying on obfuscation instead of design > Obfuscation buys time. Server authority removes whole classes of cheats. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is the most important rule of game security? + Never trust the client; decide on the server - Encrypt every file the game uses - Hide the game's code with obfuscation - Run the game with administrator rights > Encryption and obfuscation only slow tampering down; server authority makes it irrelevant for what matters. Anything on the player's machine can be changed, so decisions that affect others must be made or checked on the server. ? How do you verify the integrity of your own shipped files and updates? + Hash manifests, Authenticode signing, and signed updates - Checking each file's size when the game starts - Asking the player to reinstall when something looks wrong - Storing all files inside the exe > Signing proves who made a file and that it has not changed since. Also load DLLs only by full path from your own folder. ? What are the costs of kernel-mode anti-cheat? - None; it runs invisibly with no effect on players - It makes games run faster, which some players dislike - It only works on older versions of Windows + Players must trust it fully, and its bugs can crash the system > It sits at the highest privilege level, with all the risks of any kernel driver. It also handles personal data, with the privacy obligations that brings. ? Why can client-side protection never fully stop tampering? + It runs on the player's own machine, which they control completely - Because clients are always slower than servers - It can, if it is obfuscated enough > Protection there can only raise the cost. ? In an authoritative-server design, what do clients send? - Their positions and health, which the server trusts + Their inputs, which the server validates and simulates to decide the results - Nothing; the server guesses > The server owns the game state. ? What does code signing an update prove? - That it has no bugs - That it runs faster + Who published it, and that it is unchanged > The updater checks the signature before installing. ```
ideas:
- Add a hash manifest to Delve's release folder and a check at startup that reports any file that does not match.
- Change Delve's leaderboard design (on paper) from submitting scores to submitting replays, and list what the server must check.
- Read the anti-cheat and privacy section of a game's terms of service and list what it says is collected.

cards.q: What is the most important rule of game security?
cards.a:
Never trust the client; decide on the server

Encryption and obfuscation only slow tampering down; server authority makes it irrelevant for what matters. Anything on the player's machine can be changed, so decisions that affect others must be made or checked on the server.

cards.q: How do you verify the integrity of your own shipped files and updates?
cards.a:
Hash manifests, Authenticode signing, and signed updates

Signing proves who made a file and that it has not changed since. Also load DLLs only by full path from your own folder.

cards.q: What are the costs of kernel-mode anti-cheat?
cards.a:
Players must trust it fully, and its bugs can crash the system

It sits at the highest privilege level, with all the risks of any kernel driver. It also handles personal data, with the privacy obligations that brings.

cards.a:

Protection there can only raise the cost.

cards.a:
Their inputs, which the server validates and simulates to decide the results

The server owns the game state.

cards.a:
Who published it, and that it is unchanged

The updater checks the signature before installing.
